## Background

Many organisms live in close proximity (on or in) to other organisms.
These *symbionts* may have important impacts on their *hosts*, with
examples ranging from parasites to mutualists. These impacts may include
may include resource extraction, leading to reduced energy for hosts,
but also may include changes in host behavior. Importantly, potential
hosts may recognize the threat of parasitism and alter their behavior to
minimize this interaction.

@reyes2026 explored this question in exposing burying beetles
(*Nicrophorus nepalensis*) and their symbiotic mites (*Poechilochirus
carabi*. These mites attach to beetles to "follow" them to the carcasses
they consume(this is called *phoresy*). This is considered a *commensal*
interaction, meaning the beetles are not harmed but the mites gain a
benefit. However, once they arrive at a carcass, mite presence may
benefit the beetles by consuming competing species like blowfies, but
they also may reduce beetle population growth by consuming beetle eggs
and larvae. Other unknown impacts may also exist. Given this, the
scientists wanted to know if the presence of mites during movement
towards a carcass (the phoretic interaction) changed beetle behavior. To
"disentangle" this, beetles were exposed to

-   no mites (c: control)
-   mites only prior to introduction to a carcass (mites were then
    removed) (r: removed)
-   mites prior to introduction to a carcass and during time in carcass
    (mites were not removed) (m: mites)

Various outcomes were then considered. You are asked to help analyze the data.

[![Experimental design and timeline (Fig 1 from Reyes et
al)](gr1_lrg.jpg)](https://www.cell.com/iscience/fulltext/S2589-0042(26)01957-7)

## Design

Pulling in data and making columns (following published R script).

```{r}
data<-read.csv("mite_exp_data_combined.csv",header=T)
data$avg_larva_mass<-data$tot.weight/data$larvae
data$larval_density <- data$larvae/data$carc.wt
```

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
datanew <- data %>%
  mutate(across(c(carc.wt,avg_larva_mass, tot.weight, larvae, Mass_change_1, Mass_change_2, lifespan), as.numeric))
datanew <- subset(datanew, larvae != 0 & !is.na(larvae))
datanew$bl<-as.factor(datanew$bl)
datanew$pair<-as.factor(datanew$pair)
datanew$tr <- factor(datanew$tr, 
                       levels = c("c", "r", "m"))
str(datanew)
summary(datanew)
```

What they analyzed:

-   \# of larvae (reproductive success)

    -   model=glmer(larvae\~tr+carc.wt+clutch.size+(1\|bl/pair),poisson,data=data)

-   brood size v mite number in m group

    -   datam=data\[data\$tr=="m",\] ; only for mite treatment

    -   model=glmer(larvae\~carc.wt+mite.number+(1\|bl),poisson,data=datam)
        model=glmer(mite.number\~carc.wt+larvae+(1\|bl),poisson,data=datam)

    -   model=glmer(tot.weight\~carc.wt+mite.number+(1\|bl),gaussian,data=datam)

        -   tot.weight is total brood mass

    -   model=glmer(tot.weight\~tr+carc.wt+(1\|bl/pair),gaussian,data=data\[data\$larvae!="0",\])

-   avg larval mass

    -   model=glmer(avg_larva_mass\~tr\*larvae+carc.wt+(1\|bl/pair),gaussian,data=data)

    -   model=glmer(Mass_change_1\~tr\*clutch.size+carc.wt+(1\|bl/pair),gaussian,data=data)

    -   model=glmer(Mass_change_2\~tr\*larvae+carc.wt+(1\|bl/pair),gaussian,data=data)

-   mite \# relationship

    -   datam=data\[data\$tr=="m",\]

    -   model1 \<- glmer(larvae \~
        mite.number+clutch.size+carc.wt+(1\|bl), poisson, data = datam)

    -   model2 \<- glmer(avg_larva_mass \~
        mite.number+larvae+carc.wt+(1\|bl), gaussian, data = datam)

Let's do questions focused on:

-   average larval mass under each condition

    -   ignore blocks, ids, etc

```{r}
    datanew$treatment <- datanew$tr
    datanew$number_of_larvae <- datanew$larvae
    datanew$average_larval_mass_g <- datanew$avg_larva_mass
    datanew$mite_number <- datanew$mite.number
    write.csv(datanew[,names(datanew) %in% c("treatment", "number_of_larvae","average_larval_mass_g")], "experimental_data.csv", row.names = F)
    write.csv(datanew[,names(datanew)%in% c("treatment", "number_of_larvae", "lifespan")], "lifespan_info.csv", row.names = F)
     write.csv(datanew[datanew$treatment == "m", names(datanew) %in% c("mite_number", "number_of_larvae")], "mite_number_info.csv", row.names = F)   
```

-   brood size vs mite number in m group

-   relationship between avg larval mass and number of larvae

-   impact of brood size on lifespan

    -   ancova wiht treatment

-   probability of success

    -   Across all three treatment groups, the majority of females
        produced eggs, with rates ranging from 68.4% to 73.0% (control:
        54/74, 73.0%; mite-cue: 52/73, 71.2%; with-mite: 54/79, 68.4%).
        There was no significant difference in the probability of egg
        production across the treatments (Chi-square test: X2 = 0.40,
        d.f. = 2, *p* = 0.817). However, the probability of breeding
        success varied across the treatments (control: 32/74, 43.2%;
        mite-cue: 34/73, 46.6%; with-mite: 43/79, 54.4%; Pearson’s
        Chi-squared test: X2 = 7.58, d.f. = 2, *p* = 0.023).
